name: Udayy
epitaph: Closed early. Handed back the change.
oneLiner: Live online classes in maths and English for kids aged 6 to 11, in tiny groups of three to five.
causeOfDeath: Its demand came from lockdowns. When schools reopened, getting new parents became very costly and kids drifted away, so the founders shut it down.
moneyNote: Co-founder Saumya Yadav said Udayy raised around $13 M (Inc42 cites $13.5 M from her posts), used about $4–4.5 M, and returned around $8–8.5 M to investors. No valuation was published. Figures were reported in US dollars, so no conversion was needed.
inOneMinute: Udayy grew fast in lockdown, running **400+ live classrooms a day**. In February 2022 it raised about $10 million.
About **seven weeks later** the founders decided to shut down, even though they still had months of money left.
They refunded 3,000+ parents, found jobs for staff, and **returned about $8–8.5 million** to investors.
killerLine: When the data says no, **fail fast**. Stopping early can return money, jobs and trust that a slow death would burn.

chapters.title: The idea
chapters.body: Saumya Yadav, Mahak Garg and Karan Varshney started Udayy in Gurugram in 2019. Their target was small children, aged 6 to 11, in grades 1 to 5. Udayy ran **live online classes for just three to five kids**, in mathematical thinking and speaking skills. It used a "flipped classroom" (kids explore at their own pace first, then the teacher guides). A free app gave daily worksheets. Yadav's pitch was blunt: "An outdated education system is failing Indian parents and children." Then Covid shut every school in India. Suddenly parents everywhere were looking for exactly this, at home, on a screen.

chapters.title: The rise
chapters.body: In January 2021, Udayy raised a **$2.5 million seed round** led by Alpha Wave Incubation and Info Edge Ventures, with CRED founder Kunal Shah among the angels. It said it had users in more than 45 cities and towns and ran **over 400 classrooms every day**. It claimed 97% of paying parents renewed. Later it said it had run more than 1.3 lakh (130,000) classes with over 200 teachers. In February 2022 it raised about $10 million more, led by Norwest Venture Partners. On paper, this was a startup going up. As Yadav later said, "We started during the pandemic and were doing very well."

chapters.title: The cracks
chapters.body: Inside, the trouble had started in **July 2021**, as schools began to reopen. Kids had less time and energy for online classes after a full school day. Parents told the team the classes were good, but, as one put it, "my kid and I are just tired of zoom meetings." Customer acquisition cost (what you spend on ads and sales to win one new customer) hit an all-time high, while fewer families renewed. The founders tried pivots for six to eight months. Offline centres were too expensive. The free app was popular but hard to make money from. Schools treated edtech **as competition, not a helper**.

chapters.title: The fall
chapters.body: In late March 2022, with **months of runway** (money to keep running) still left, the founders decided to close. On 4 April they told the whole team at a town hall. Classes ended about two weeks later. The team tracked refunds for **more than 3,000 parents**, and only 20–30 could not be reached. Yadav said they contacted about 30 companies and found jobs for all their employees, who also got severance pay. Then they **returned around $8–8.5 million** to investors. When the news went public about two months later, nearly every staff member already had a new job. It is one of the cleanest shutdowns in Indian startups.

charts.title: Where the money went
charts.takeaway: By stopping early, Udayy gave back about two-thirds of everything it raised.

mistakes.title: Mistaking a lockdown habit for lasting demand
mistakes.explain: Udayy's growth came from kids stuck at home. Once schools reopened, **the need shrank**, and parents were "tired of zoom meetings". The product was liked; the moment had passed. A founder should ask early: **would people still want this if the special situation ended?**

mistakes.title: Raising a big round after the warning signs had begun
mistakes.explain: Trouble started in July 2021, yet Udayy raised about $10 million in February 2022 and decided to shut seven weeks later. To their credit, they returned most of it. But a fundraise is a good moment to **test your own story hard**: if the numbers had been bending for months, **what has changed?**

mistakes.title: Getting expensive to win, easy to lose
mistakes.explain: Customer acquisition cost hit an all-time high while renewals fell. When each new family costs more and stays less, **growth itself becomes a loss**. Udayy watched this closely, which is why it could stop in time. Many startups only look at total users and **miss this until the money is gone**.

mistakes.title: A free app with no path to money
mistakes.explain: The free worksheet app drew heavy use but was hard to monetize. Free products can be great for reach, but only if you know **who will pay, and for what**. Otherwise popularity just adds server bills and support work while the paid business shrinks.

warningSigns: Would customers drop you if the situation that made you popular ended tomorrow?
Is your cost to win one customer rising month after month?
Are fewer customers renewing than six months ago?
Have your last three pivots failed to fix the same core number?
Are users happy with you but too tired or busy to keep using you?

lessons.title: Track cost-per-customer and renewals monthly
lessons.detail: Make one simple chart: what you spend to win a customer, and how many stay. When the lines cross the wrong way for a few months, take it seriously.

lessons.title: Set a 'stop' rule before you need it
lessons.detail: Decide in advance what result, by what date, would make you shut down or change course. It is far easier to follow a rule than to make the call in the middle of hope and fear.

lessons.title: Close while you still have money
lessons.detail: Udayy shut down with months of runway, so it could pay severance, refund parents and return cash. Waiting until zero would have made all of that impossible.

lessons.title: Plan the shutdown like a launch
lessons.detail: List everyone you owe: staff, customers, vendors, investors. Make a sheet, assign owners, and tick each one off. A clean ending keeps doors open for your next startup.

lessons.title: Help your team land somewhere
lessons.detail: Udayy contacted about 30 companies and found jobs for all its staff. Your reputation with employees is the most valuable thing you take into your next company.

quote.text: We had the choice to fail fast or fail slow.
quote.context: In her LinkedIn post about shutting down Udayy, 2022

afterlife.text: Udayy ended its classes in April 2022, and the shutdown became public in June, by when nearly all staff had new jobs and almost all customers had been refunded. Mahak Garg wrote that she would start again, despite the outcome. Inc42's company database still lists the legal entity (Skorion Technologies) as private, with ₹24.5 crore revenue in FY25 after shifting its offerings; we could not confirm what it does now.
